newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore economy set for Q2 upturn - economist.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economy set for Q2 upturn - economist.

text.p: Singapore's economy will start a robust recovery in the second quarter and grow 7.3 percent in 1997, beating the official government estimate of between five and seven percent, a senior economist said on Wednesday.
"The outlook is quite bright over the next quarter and the rest of the year," Neil Saker, head of regional economic research at SocGen-Crosby, told reporters.
Saker said the 7.3 percent estimate erred on the side of caution: "If anything we think growth will exceed that."
Electronics, business and financial services and exports would all be major components of the recovery, he said.
Singapore's economy grew 3.8 percent in the first quarter of 1997 against 11.5 percent in the same period of 1996, with many analysts not predicting upturn until the third quarter of 1997.
Saker said the growth would come earlier and be fuelled by manufacturing, despite the sector suffering a 6.7 percent fall in the first quarter of 1997 against a 13.6 percent surge a year earlier.
Most of the first quarter drop was caused by a slump in electronics, but Saker said electronics would recover to become the main manufacturing driver.

Saker said new electronics orders from the United States were up 12.9 percent in the first quarter of 1997 and Malaysia's electronics production was up by 32.5 percent in March 1997, compared to 4.8 percent in August 1996.
Business and financial services were also likely to emerge as key drivers for the Singapore economy in future.
"Business services will continue to register very strong growth and are becoming quite an important part of the economic revival," Saker said.
Business services grew 10.5 percent in the first quarter of 1997, up from 9.1 percent a year earlier.
Saker said pressure to deregulate financial services and allow trade in new financial instruments was growing.

"Singapore is reluctant to deregulate but the developments in the rest of the region will force the pace," he said, pointing to Malaysia's authorisation of financial futures trading as one motivating factor.
Saker said he saw Singapore's regional competitors as the main longer term threat.
"Wages are high, land costs are high. The government must focus on how to tackle these competitive issues," he said.
